alt: Fruit example of data augmentation: one apple image becomes six images (original, rotated 20 degrees, flipped horizontally, zoomed in, increased brightness, small noise added) and all are still labeled Apple. The model becomes more accurate on unseen apple images.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Data augmentation: the new concept (create new training samples by modifying the existing data; the images still represent the same object) and why we need it (increase the size of the training dataset, reduce overfitting, improve generalization, make the model robust, improve prediction accuracy).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The problem with a small dataset: deep learning models need a lot of data, a small dataset makes the model memorize background, lighting, camera angle and noise instead of the object and causes overfitting (training accuracy very high, testing accuracy low), and collecting more data is time-consuming, expensive, difficult and sometimes impossible.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Six common data augmentation techniques on an apple image (rotation, flipping, zooming, cropping, brightness adjustment, noise addition), each with what it does, and the data augmentation flow from the original image through each technique to multiple new training images.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Bias-variance trade-off: as model complexity increases, bias decreases and variance increases; the goal is the right balance. A graph of error against model complexity shows bias falling, variance rising and a total error curve with a minimum at the good fit between underfit and overfit.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Benefits of batch normalization: faster training, stable learning, allows a higher learning rate, reduces internal covariate shift and slightly reduces overfitting, each with a small picture.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Batch normalization: the new concept (a technique that normalizes the outputs of a layer before passing them to the next layer so that values stay within a similar range) which makes training faster and more stable.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Scale using gamma (gamma times x-hat), shift using beta (gamma x-hat plus beta), the final batch normalization formula y equals gamma times (x minus mu) divided by square root of (sigma squared plus epsilon) plus beta with the meaning of each symbol, and the complete flow: input, mean, variance, normalize, multiply by gamma, add beta, output to the next layer.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Where batch normalization is placed: input, dense or convolution layer, batch normalization, activation function (ReLU), next layer, applied before the activation function. A fruit example shows hidden outputs 20, 50, 100, 150 with very different ranges becoming -1.1, -0.4, 0.5, 1.0 after batch normalization.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The problem of internal covariate shift: in a deep network the output of one layer is the input to the next and the weights keep changing, so the inputs to each layer keep changing, training becomes slow and unstable. A diagram of two hidden layers is shown.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Batch normalization step by step: what is a batch (a small group of training samples), what is normalization (bringing values into a similar range), step 1 calculate the mean (example 2, 4, 6, 8 gives mean 5), step 2 calculate the variance, and step 3 normalize the values to mean about 0 and variance about 1.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Training without batch normalization (changing outputs between layers, slow training) compared with training with batch normalization (outputs are normalized before the next layer, so learning is faster), and how batch normalization improves training with loss curves showing slow versus fast convergence.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Causes and solutions of underfitting and overfitting. Underfitting causes: model too simple, too few epochs, learning rate too high, insufficient features, training stopped too early; fixes: more epochs, more complexity, better features, appropriate learning rate. Overfitting causes: model too complex, too many epochs, small dataset, too many parameters, noise; fixes: more data, data augmentation, early stopping, dropout, L1, L2, reduce complexity.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Dropout: the new concept (a regularization technique that randomly turns off some neurons during training; dropped neurons do not take part in forward propagation, backpropagation or weight updates) and a flow from training data, randomly drop some neurons, remaining neurons learn, model learns better. Each iteration uses a slightly different network.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Example of training a network without dropout (all neurons active, some neurons depend heavily on one neuron, and if it is wrong many others become wrong) and with dropout during training (some neurons turned off, other neurons learn useful features like shape, texture, size and color, so the model becomes stronger and generalizes better).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The same network drawn without dropout and with dropout during training: input layer, hidden layer and output layer, where crossed-out neurons are dropped.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Dropout in the training phase (iterations 1, 2, 3 with some neurons off and a random network every iteration, which prevents overfitting) and in the testing phase (all neurons on, the complete network is used, final predictions).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Advantages of dropout (reduces overfitting, improves generalization, prevents neuron dependency, makes the network more robust, simple and widely used) and disadvantages (training becomes slightly slower, choosing the correct dropout rate is important, a very high dropout may cause underfitting, usually applied only during training).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A table of dropout rates p: p equals 0 (no neurons dropped, higher chance of overfitting), 0.2 (one neuron dropped, small regularization), 0.5 (half the neurons dropped, most common, good balance) and 0.8 (most neurons dropped, the model learns very little, may lead to underfitting), each with a row of green and crossed neurons.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How dropout solves the problem: during training it randomly selects some neurons and switches them off, different neurons are dropped in every iteration, the model cannot memorize the training data and every neuron learns useful patterns independently. Random drop gives less dependency, general patterns and less overfitting.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Dropout in the training phase (random neurons are turned off, different neurons are dropped in every iteration, helps reduce overfitting) and in the testing phase (no neurons are dropped, all neurons are active, the complete network is used for prediction).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Why dropout prevents overfitting: without dropout one neuron may depend heavily on another and a wrong pattern spreads to many neurons; with dropout neurons cannot depend on each other because any neuron may be dropped at any time, so each learns useful features independently and the model is stronger.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Early stopping: the new concept (a regularization technique that stops the training process automatically when the model stops improving on the validation data, at the best epoch) and why we need it (prevent overfitting, stop unnecessary training, save training time, improve generalization, select the best model automatically).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Example table of early stopping with patience 3: validation loss by epoch 1 to 7 is 0.90, 0.70, 0.55, 0.48 (best model), 0.49 (wait 1), 0.50 (wait 2), 0.51 (stop training, patience 3). No improvement for 3 consecutive epochs stops the training.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A graph of loss against epochs: the training loss falls steadily while the validation loss falls and then rises; a vertical line at the lowest validation loss marks the best epoch and the stop-here point.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Patience is the number of epochs the model waits before stopping. With patience 3, epochs 1, 2 and 3 with no improvement stop the training; patience prevents stopping too early because of small fluctuations.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The problem: training for too many epochs makes the model memorize the training data (training accuracy very high, validation accuracy decreases). Why too many epochs cause overfitting (it learns noise, outliers and unnecessary details), and why dropout, L1 and L2 cannot completely solve it; the simplest solution is early stopping.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How early stopping solves the problem: the model checks the validation loss after every epoch and stops if it does not improve for several consecutive epochs. A graph of loss shows the best epoch where the validation loss is lowest while the training loss keeps falling.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Elastic Net example for an apple: before, the weights are shape 8, color 6, texture 0.4, background 0.2; after, shape 5, color 4, texture 0.2, background 0. The background is removed, shape and color remain with smaller weights and texture remains smaller because it is useful.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Elastic Net loss: original loss equals prediction error; the Elastic Net loss is total loss equals prediction loss plus lambda 1 times the sum of absolute weights plus lambda 2 times the sum of squared weights, where lambda 1 controls the L1 penalty and lambda 2 the L2 penalty.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Easy diagram of model complexity with three plots of data points: underfit (a straight line, too simple, can't capture the pattern), good fit (a smooth curve, just right, captures the pattern) and overfit (a wiggly curve, too complex, fits noise also).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Summary table for underfitting, good fit and overfitting: bias and variance (high bias low variance, balanced, low bias high variance), training error (high, low, very low), testing error (high, low, high), model complexity (too simple, correct, too complex) and what the model learns (too little, correctly, memorizes data).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Comparison table of underfitting, good fit and overfitting on model complexity, training accuracy, testing accuracy, whether it learns the pattern and generalization.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Training accuracy versus validation accuracy: underfitting has low training and low validation accuracy, good fit has high and high, overfitting has very high training accuracy and low validation accuracy.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Fruit example of regularization: without regularization the model memorizes a small black spot, exact lighting and background color, so a new apple without the black spot is predicted Not Apple; with regularization the model learns shape, color and texture, so the new apple is predicted Apple.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: General idea of adding a penalty: without regularization, loss equals prediction error and the model only tries to reduce the prediction error; with regularization, total loss equals prediction error plus regularization penalty, so the model tries to reduce the prediction error and keep the weights small and simple. This helps reduce overfitting.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How regularization solves the problem: it adds a penalty to the loss function, so if the model creates very large or unnecessary weights it gets an extra penalty. Very large weights are discouraged, the model becomes simpler, it learns important features instead of noise and performance on unseen data improves. A balance scale shows prediction error and penalty on weights making total loss.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L1 regularization (Lasso): the new concept (reduces overfitting by adding the sum of the absolute values of all weights to the loss function) with goals to reduce unnecessary weights, remove unimportant features, build a simpler model and improve generalization. Key idea: penalize large weights, smaller weights, simpler model, less overfitting.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L1 fruit example for an apple: before L1 the weights are shape 8, color 6, texture 0.4, background 0.2; after L1 they are 7.4, 5.5, 0 and 0. Texture and background weights become 0 so only important features (shape and color) remain.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The teacher's overview of L1 regularization (Lasso: absolute value of weights, can make some weights exactly 0, feature selection; before and after weights with some zero) and L2 regularization (Ridge: square of the weights, reduces large weights but usually doesn't make them zero, most commonly used in deep learning), with diamond-shaped and circular constraint pictures.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L1 penalty calculation: weights W1 equals 6, W2 equals minus 4, W3 equals 2 and W4 equals minus 1, so the L1 penalty is the sum |6| + |-4| + |2| + |-1| = 6 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 13. Large weights create a larger penalty, shown with a bar chart.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How L1 solves the problem and its formula: L1 adds a penalty based on the absolute value of every weight; if a weight becomes very large the penalty increases, the optimizer reduces the weight, some unnecessary weights become 0, the model becomes simpler and overfitting reduces. Original loss equals prediction error; L1 regularized loss equals prediction loss plus lambda times the sum of absolute weights.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L1 weight update process: large weight, large penalty, higher total loss, the optimizer reduces the weight, small weight, some weights become 0, with a vertical line of weight values moving toward 0.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Don't confuse L1 and L2: penalty term (absolute value versus square), effect on weights (some weights become 0 versus small but usually not 0), feature selection (performs it versus does not) and also called (Lasso versus Ridge).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L2 regularization (Ridge): the new concept (reduces overfitting by adding the sum of the squares of all weights to the loss; instead of making weights exactly 0, it reduces all weights so the model becomes simpler while still using every feature) and why it is called Ridge.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L2 formula: original loss equals prediction error; L2 regularized loss is total loss equals prediction loss plus lambda times the sum of squared weights. Larger weights give a larger square and a larger penalty.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L2 fruit example: before L2 the weights are shape 8, color 6, texture 3, size 2; after L2 they are 5, 4, 2 and 1. No weight becomes 0, all features are still used but their influence is reduced.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: L2 penalty calculation: weights 5, minus 3, 2 and minus 1 give 5 squared + (-3) squared + 2 squared + (-1) squared = 25 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 39. Large weights contribute much more to the penalty.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How L2 solves the problem: a large weight gives a large square and a large penalty, so the optimizer reduces the weight, the model becomes simpler and overfitting reduces. Unlike L1, weights usually become very small but not exactly zero, shown with a bar chart of shrinking weights.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: The role of lambda: lambda equal to 0 (no regularization, model becomes very complex, memorizes, overfitting), small lambda (recommended: weights controlled, important features learned, noise ignored, good generalization) and large lambda (weights become too small, the model cannot learn enough patterns, underfitting), each with the fruit example.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Effect of lambda in three tables: on model complexity (very complex, balanced, very simple), on the weights (large, moderate, very small) and on underfitting and overfitting (overfitting at lambda 0, good fit at small lambda, underfitting at large lambda).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: A U-shaped graph of error against regularization strength: no regularization (lambda 0) overfits, the best lambda is small and gives a good fit, and too much regularization (large lambda) underfits.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Training loss versus validation loss over epochs for underfitting (both remain high), good fit (both decrease and stay close) and overfitting (training loss keeps decreasing but validation loss starts increasing).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How noise injection solves the problem: during training the input data goes through a step that adds small random noise before the neural network and prediction. Without noise injection the model overfits; with it there is better generalization. The model learns to ignore unimportant variations and focus on important features.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Types of noise injection: input noise (small random noise added to the input data), weight noise (small random values added to the weights, for example 0.80 plus 0.02 gives 0.82) and hidden layer (activation) noise (noise added to the output of hidden neurons).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Two plots with the legend training data (blue circles) and model prediction (red triangles). Underfitting learns too little: the model is too simple to capture the pattern, with high error on training and testing data. Overfitting learns too much: the model is too complex and memorizes the training data, with low training error but high testing error.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Fruit example for a CNN: an apple can appear at different positions in the image (top, center, bottom). Instead of learning different weights for each position, a CNN uses the same filter (shared weights) everywhere, so the model can recognize the apple anywhere.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Main idea of parameter sharing: without parameter sharing each input connection has a different weight (W1, W2, W3, W4) giving more parameters; with parameter sharing the connections use one shared weight W giving fewer parameters.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: How to reduce high bias (underfitting): increase model complexity, train for more epochs, add more useful features, use a more powerful model. How to reduce high variance (overfitting): increase training data, use dropout, apply L1 and L2 regularization, use early stopping, reduce model complexity.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Why the optimizer chooses smaller weights: two models give the same prediction error 4. Model A has weight 25, a high penalty and a high total loss; model B has weight 5, a low penalty and a low total loss. The optimizer chooses model B because it has a lower total loss.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Training error versus testing error without and with regularization. Without regularization the training error keeps decreasing while the testing error starts increasing (overfitting). With regularization the training error is slightly higher but the testing error becomes lower, giving better generalization.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Weight decay: what it is (a regularization technique that reduces or shrinks the weights after every update during training; simple definition: gradually reducing the size of the weights) shown with a tall red bar becoming a small green bar, and why we need it (prevent large weights, reduce overfitting, improve generalization, make the model simpler, improve prediction on unseen data).
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Weight update with and without weight decay: without it the old weight 2.5 goes through the gradient update to a new weight 9.2 which becomes very large; with weight decay the old weight 2.5 goes to 2.3 and then to a smaller weight 2.0 that stays small.
author: Deep Learning faculty

alt: Weight penalty concept: large weights lead to a large penalty, a higher total loss, the optimizer reduces the weights, a simpler model and better generalization, with a barbell and a high-penalty gauge.
author: Deep Learning faculty
